post_title: The 1% rule is dead. Here's what replaced it.
example: Example numbers for illustration · 25% down · 7% · 30-year loan

lines.voice: The old rule: a rental should bring in {one percent|1%} of its price, every month.
A {three hundred thousand dollar|$300,000} house? {Three thousand|$3,000} a month in rent.
In a lot of markets, that house rents for closer to {two thousand|$2,000}.
That's {point six seven percent|0.67%}. It fails the rule.
Worse, it ignores your *interest* rate, *insurance*, property *taxes*, and *repairs*.
The stuff that decides if you make money.
What replaced it? *Real* monthly cash flow.
Rent, {two thousand|$2,000}. Minus the mortgage, {fourteen ninety-seven|$1,497}. Taxes and insurance, {four fifty|$450}. Repairs, vacancy and CapEx, {three hundred|$300}.
So what price works? Drop it to about {two hundred fifty thousand|$250K},
and the same house breaks even.

caption:
The 1% rule is dead. Here's what replaced it.

Old rule: rent should be 1% of the price every month. A $300K house → $3,000/mo.

In a lot of markets that house rents for ~$2,000. And the rule ignores the things that decide whether you make money: your rate, insurance, taxes, repairs.

What replaced it: real monthly cash flow.
Rent $2,000
− Mortgage $1,497 ($225K loan, 7%, 30 yr)
− Taxes + insurance $450
− Repairs/vacancy/CapEx $300
= −$247/mo

Break-even price on the same house ≈ $250K. The rule isn't the problem. The price is.

Example numbers for illustration only. Your market, rate and costs will differ.
